::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[Definition of differentiability at one point](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/3575523/definition-of-differentiability-at-one-point), asked by [Daniel Oscar](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/571152/daniel-oscar) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2020-03-09; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> My Multivariable Calculus notes state that, in order for a function of the type $\mathbb{R}^2\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ to be differentiable at a given point, the limit $$\lim _{h,\:k\to 0}\left(\frac{E\left(h,\:k\right)\:}{\:\sqrt{h^2+k^2}}\right)=0$$ Where $$f\left(a+h,\:b+k\right)-f\left(a,\:b\right)=h\cdot \frac{\partial }{\partial x}\left(a,\:b\right)+k\cdot \frac{\partial }{\partial y}\left(a,\:b\right)+E\left(h,\:k\right)$$ But everyone just expect us to memorize this and reproduce it on the exam. What does this really mean? Why does the limit must approach $0$?
:::

For a fixed point $(a,b)$ the function
$$L(a+h,b+k) = f(a,b) + h \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a,b) + k \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(a,b)$$
is a (affine) linear function that satisfies $L(a,b) = f(a,b)$, $\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}(a,b) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}(a,b)$, and $\frac{\partial L}{\partial y}(a,b) = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}(a,b)$.  So $L$ is essentially the *best possible* linear approximation to $f$ near $(a,b)$.

But how good an approximation is it?  That depends how close $f$ is to $L$ in a neighborhood of $(a,b)$.  We want the difference $f-L = E$ to go to zero as $(h,k) \to (0,0)$.  But not *just* go to zero, go to zero faster than $h$ and $k$ go to zero.  Or equivalently, faster than the length $\sqrt{h^2+k^2}$ goes to zero. That is why we take the quotient and require it to have a limit of zero.

Heuristically, $f$ is differentiable at $(a,b)$ if the graph of $L$ matches our intuitive notions of “tangent plane to the graph of $f$” at $(a,b)$.
